title: Boosting IV — LightGBM & CatBoost

blocks.t: Where these fit
The one-line summary

All three are gradient boosting on decision trees. They differ only in
how a single tree is grown and what preprocessing is built in.

XGBoost — level-wise growth, exact or histogram splits, best-tested,
the safe default.

LightGBM — leaf-wise growth + GOSS + EFB. Fastest on large/wide data,
overfits small data if left unchecked.

CatBoost — ordered boosting + ordered target statistics + symmetric
trees. Best when you have many high-cardinality categorical columns, and works
well with almost no tuning.
LightGBM: three ideas
Leaf-wise (best-first) growth

XGBoost grows level by level: split every node at depth $d$ before
touching depth $d+1$. That is symmetric and easy to parallelise, but it wastes
effort splitting nodes that were already almost pure.

LightGBM grows leaf by leaf: of all current leaves, split the
single one that gives the largest loss reduction. The tree becomes lopsided —
deep where the data is hard, shallow where it is easy. For the same number of
leaves it reaches a lower training loss, which is both its advantage and its
danger.

blocks.cap:
The same budget spent two ways. Level-wise keeps the tree balanced;
leaf-wise spends depth only where the loss says it pays.

blocks.t:
Because leaf-wise growth is greedy about loss, LightGBM overfits small
datasets far more readily than XGBoost. The control is num_leaves, not
max_depth. Rule of thumb: num_leaves $< 2^{\texttt{max\_depth}}$,
and on a few thousand rows keep it at 15–31, not the default 31–127. The right
panel of the next figure shows train AUC hitting 1.0 while test AUC falls.
GOSS — Gradient-based One-Side Sampling

Rows with a small $|g_i|$ are already well fitted; they contribute almost
nothing to the next split's gain. GOSS keeps the top $a\cdot n$ rows by
$|g_i|$, randomly samples $b\cdot n$ of the rest, and multiplies the
sampled small-gradient rows' gradients by $\frac{1-a}{b}$ to keep the estimate
unbiased:

with $A$ the kept large-gradient rows and $B$ the sampled small-gradient rows.
Without the $\frac{1-a}{b}$ factor the split criterion would be biased towards
hard rows and the tree would chase outliers.

This is not the same as subsample, which drops rows
uniformly at random. GOSS drops preferentially the rows that carry no
information, so it loses less accuracy per row discarded.
EFB — Exclusive Feature Bundling

After one-hot encoding, most columns are almost all zeros, and two one-hot
columns from the same original variable are never non-zero on the same
row — they are mutually exclusive. EFB packs such columns into a single
bundle by offsetting their value ranges (feature $B$'s bins are shifted above
feature $A$'s), so one histogram covers both. A dataset with 10{,}000 sparse
columns can collapse to a few hundred bundles, and histogram building is
$O(\#\text{bundles} \times n)$ rather than $O(\#\text{features}\times n)$.
Finding the optimal bundling is graph colouring — NP-hard — so LightGBM
uses a greedy approximation with a small allowed conflict rate.

blocks.cap:
Measured on 40{,}000 rows $\times$ 40 features, 300 trees, identical
learning rate. Accuracy is essentially tied; wall-clock is not. Right panel:
num_leaves is the overfitting dial.

blocks.t: CatBoost: the leakage problem, solved
Why naive target encoding is broken

The obvious way to encode a categorical column is to replace each level with
the mean target for that level. For a high-cardinality column — customer ID,
postcode, product SKU — each level has only a handful of rows, so
a row's own label dominates its own encoding. The feature then predicts
the training labels almost perfectly and carries no signal at all on new data.
The model learns to lean on it, and validation collapses.

blocks.cap:
A category built from pure random noise. Naive target encoding
separates the classes cleanly — a fiction. Ordered target statistics show the
truth: no separation.

blocks.t: Ordered target statistics

Fix a random permutation $\sigma$ of the training rows. For row $i$, encode its
category using only the rows that come before it in $\sigma$:

where $p$ is the global target mean (the prior) and $a>0$ its weight. Row $i$'s
own label never enters its own encoding, so the feature is honest. CatBoost
uses several permutations to reduce the variance for early rows, which would
otherwise be encoded almost entirely by the prior.
Ordered boosting

The same leakage exists in boosting itself, and nobody noticed for years.
When we compute the residual $y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$, the model $F_{m-1}$ was
trained on a set that includes row $i$. So the residual is
systematically too small — the model has already partly memorised that row.
CatBoost calls this prediction shift: the gradient distribution during
training does not match the one at inference.

CatBoost's fix mirrors the encoding fix. It maintains models
$M_1,\dots,M_n$ where $M_k$ is trained only on the first $k$ rows of a
permutation, and computes row $i$'s residual using $M_{i-1}$ — a model that
has never seen row $i$. This is expensive done literally, so the
implementation approximates it with a logarithmic number of models.
Symmetric (oblivious) trees

CatBoost's trees are oblivious: every node at the same depth uses the
same feature and threshold. A depth-6 tree is therefore just 6
comparisons producing a 6-bit index into a table of $2^6$ leaf values. This
is heavily regularising — the tree cannot adapt its structure per branch —
and makes inference extremely fast, which is why CatBoost is popular in
latency-sensitive production. It also means CatBoost usually needs more trees
than LightGBM for the same fit.
Choosing between them
Practical rule

Wide numeric data and millions of rows $\to$ LightGBM.
Many high-cardinality categorical columns, or you have no time to tune $\to$
CatBoost. Anything else, or you need the most battle-tested option
$\to$ XGBoost. On most tabular problems the three land within a
fraction of a percent of each other once tuned — the choice is about data
shape and engineering constraints, not accuracy.
Code

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=50000, n_features=40, n_informative=15,
                           random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. LIGHTGBM -- sklearn API
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
clf = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
        n_estimators     = 3000,     # upper bound; early stopping decides
        learning_rate    = 0.05,
        num_leaves       = 31,       # THE dial. < 2**max_depth
        max_depth        = -1,       # -1 = unlimited; num_leaves is the real cap
        min_child_samples= 20,       # min rows per leaf -- raise on small data
        subsample        = 0.8,      # bagging_fraction
        subsample_freq   = 1,        # bag every iteration (0 disables bagging!)
        colsample_bytree = 0.8,      # feature_fraction
        reg_lambda       = 1.0,
        n_jobs           = 4,
        random_state     = 0,
        verbose          = -1)

clf.fit(Xtr, ytr,
        eval_set=[(Xte, yte)],
        eval_metric="auc",
        callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(50, verbose=False),
                   lgb.log_evaluation(0)])
print("best iter:", clf.best_iteration_,
      "AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(yte, clf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))

# GOSS -- gradient-based one-side sampling instead of random bagging
goss = lgb.LGBMClassifier(boosting_type="goss", n_estimators=500,
                          learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31,
                          top_rate=0.2,     # 'a' -- keep top 20% by |gradient|
                          other_rate=0.1,   # 'b' -- sample 10% of the rest
                          n_jobs=4, verbose=-1).fit(Xtr, ytr)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. LIGHTGBM WITH NATIVE CATEGORICALS -- no one-hot anywhere
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "num1": rng.normal(size=20000),
    "num2": rng.normal(size=20000),
    "city": pd.Categorical(rng.choice(["del", "mum", "blr", "hyd"], 20000)),
    "sku" : pd.Categorical(rng.integers(0, 900, 20000)),   # high cardinality
})
target = (df.num1 + (df.city == "blr").astype(int) * 1.5
          + rng.normal(0, 0.6, 20000) > 0).astype(int)

a, b, ya, yb = train_test_split(df, target, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
m = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=400, num_leaves=31, learning_rate=0.05,
                       n_jobs=4, verbose=-1)
# LightGBM detects the 'category' dtype automatically; you can also pass
# categorical_feature=["city", "sku"] explicitly.
m.fit(a, ya, categorical_feature=["city", "sku"])
print("LGBM native-cat AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(yb, m.predict_proba(b)[:, 1]), 4))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. CATBOOST  (pip install catboost)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# from catboost import CatBoostClassifier, Pool
#
# cat_cols = ["city", "sku"]
# train_pool = Pool(a, ya, cat_features=cat_cols)
# valid_pool = Pool(b, yb, cat_features=cat_cols)
#
# cb = CatBoostClassifier(
#         iterations       = 3000,
#         learning_rate    = 0.05,
#         depth            = 6,          # symmetric trees: 2**6 = 64 leaves
#         l2_leaf_reg      = 3.0,
#         one_hot_max_size = 10,   # <=10 levels -> one-hot; more -> ordered TS
#         random_strength  = 1.0,  # noise added to split scores (regularisation)
#         bagging_temperature = 1.0,     # Bayesian bootstrap intensity
#         boosting_type    = "Ordered",  # ordered boosting; "Plain" is faster
#         eval_metric      = "AUC",
#         early_stopping_rounds = 50,
#         verbose          = 0,
#         random_seed      = 0)
#
# cb.fit(train_pool, eval_set=valid_pool, use_best_model=True)
# print("CatBoost AUC:", cb.get_best_score()["validation"]["AUC"])
#
# # CatBoost passes RAW strings -- never LabelEncode before handing them over,
# # and never one-hot: that destroys the ordered target statistics.

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. ORDERED TARGET STATISTICS, IMPLEMENTED BY HAND
#    (this is what CatBoost does internally)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def ordered_target_encode(cat, y, prior_weight=1.0, seed=0):
    rng   = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    prior = y.mean()
    out   = np.zeros(len(y))
    total, count = {}, {}
    for i in rng.permutation(len(y)):          # a random ORDER
        c = cat[i]
        # encode using ONLY rows already seen -- never row i itself
        out[i] = (total.get(c, 0.0) + prior * prior_weight) / \
                 (count.get(c, 0)   + prior_weight)
        total[c] = total.get(c, 0.0) + y[i]
        count[c] = count.get(c, 0) + 1
    return out

noise_cat = rng.integers(0, 300, 1500)         # pure noise, 300 levels
noise_y   = rng.integers(0, 2, 1500)
naive = np.array([noise_y[noise_cat == c].mean() for c in noise_cat])  # LEAKS
safe  = ordered_target_encode(noise_cat, noise_y)
print("corr with y -- naive:", round(np.corrcoef(naive, noise_y)[0, 1], 3),
      " ordered:",             round(np.corrcoef(safe,  noise_y)[0, 1], 3))
# naive ~0.7 on a feature that is literally random; ordered ~0.0. That gap
# is the entire reason CatBoost exists.

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. FAIR COMPARISON HARNESS
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
import time, xgboost as xgb
def bench(model, name):
    t0 = time.time(); model.fit(Xtr, ytr); fit = time.time() - t0
    auc = roc_auc_score(yte, model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1])
    print(f"{name:12s} {fit:6.2f}s   AUC {auc:.4f}")

bench(xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.1,
                        tree_method="hist", n_jobs=4, verbosity=0), "XGBoost")
bench(lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=300, num_leaves=31, learning_rate=0.1,
                         n_jobs=4, verbose=-1), "LightGBM")
Everything on one page
Summary

LightGBM = three tricks.
Leaf-wise growth (split the highest-loss leaf, not the whole level) —
lower loss per leaf, higher overfitting risk, controlled by num_leaves.
GOSS — keep the top-$a$ rows by $|$gradient$|$, subsample the rest and
reweight by $\frac{1-a}{b}$ to stay unbiased.
EFB — bundle mutually-exclusive sparse columns into one histogram.

CatBoost = two leakage fixes plus oblivious trees.
Ordered target statistics — encode a category using only rows earlier
in a random permutation, plus a prior; the row's own label never touches its own
feature. Ordered boosting — compute row $i$'s residual from a model
never trained on row $i$, removing prediction shift. Oblivious trees —
one feature/threshold per depth level: strong regularisation and very fast
inference.

Gotchas: LightGBM's subsample does nothing unless
subsample_freq > 0. max_depth=-1 is unlimited, so
num_leaves is your only guard. CatBoost wants raw strings — do not
label-encode or one-hot first.
Interview corner
Q. Level-wise vs leaf-wise — which is better?

Neither universally. Leaf-wise reaches a lower training loss for a fixed leaf
budget because it spends splits where they pay most, so it is faster to a given
accuracy on large data. On small data that same greediness overfits. Level-wise
is more symmetric and implicitly regularised.
Q. How is GOSS different from row subsampling?

Subsampling drops rows uniformly. GOSS keeps all large-gradient (poorly fitted)
rows and samples only among the small-gradient ones, then up-weights those
samples by $(1-a)/b$ so the gain estimate stays unbiased. It discards mostly
rows that carry no information.
Q. Why does LightGBM overfit small datasets?

Leaf-wise growth plus a num_leaves default of 31 and
max_depth=-1 means the tree can go very deep on one branch until a leaf
holds a handful of rows. Fix: cut num_leaves to 15–31, raise
min_child_samples, add reg_lambda, use early stopping.
Q. What is target leakage in target encoding, and CatBoost's fix?

A rare category's mean target is dominated by the row's own label, so the
feature predicts train labels but nothing else. CatBoost computes the encoding
from only the rows preceding it in a random permutation, smoothed towards the
global prior — an online, leak-free estimate.
Q. What is prediction shift?

Residuals during training are computed from a model that was itself trained on
those same rows, so they are biased small relative to what happens at
inference. Ordered boosting computes row $i$'s residual from a model that never
saw row $i$, aligning the two distributions.
Q. What is an oblivious tree and why use one?

Every node at a given depth shares the same feature and threshold, so the tree
is a lookup table indexed by $d$ bits. It regularises heavily and makes
inference extremely fast and vectorisable — valuable when you serve millions
of predictions per second.
Q. When would you not use any of these?

When the data is not tabular (images, audio, long text — use deep learning),
when you need a globally interpretable model with coefficients (use regularised
linear or a single tree), when you have very few rows relative to features
(regularised linear usually wins), or when extrapolation beyond the training
range is required — trees output constants and cannot extrapolate at all.
Worked Examples
Histogram binning and CatBoost target statistics
Part 1 – LightGBM histogram binning. Feature values $[1,2,2,3,8,9,10,20]$, bucketed into $4$ equal-width bins over $[1,20]$ (width $4.75$). Bin edges: $1,\;5.75,\;10.5,\;15.25,\;20$.
Split candidates are now the 3 bin boundaries, not all 7 gaps between values. Scanning histograms of gradient sums is far cheaper on large data, which is a main source of LightGBM's speed.
Part 2 – CatBoost ordered target statistic. Category city = Mumbai. Previous rows with Mumbai: one row with label 1. Prior $0.5$, smoothing weight $a=1$:
\text{TS} = \frac{\text{sum of positive labels} + a\cdot\text{prior}}{\text{count} + a} = \frac{1 + 0.5}{1+1} = 0.75
Each row's encoding uses only rows before it in a random order, so a row never sees its own label. Naive target encoding leaks the label and inflates training scores.
